sections.text: That tumultuous sound rent the hearts of (the members of) Dhritarashtras party, making both the heaven and the earth resound.

Then, seeing the people of Dhritarashtra’s party standing arrayed and the discharge of weapons about to begin, Arjuna, the son of Pandu, whose ensign was a monkey, took up his bow and said the following to Krishna, O Lord of the earth.

Arjuna said: In the middle between the two armies, place my chariot, O Krishna, so that I may behold those who stand here desirous to fight, and know with whom I must fight, when the battle is about to commence.

We are now discussing Chapter 1, Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the Yoga of Arjunas Grief. In the first 18 verses, we have seen the situation with Dhritarashtra, the situation with Duryodhana, how Bhishma reacted, and how the Pandavas reacted. What we are basically seeing here is that anytime someone speaks, we can see his mental state.
Unless somebody speaks, we will not know whats going on. So up till now, through the very first verse, we have seen Dhritarashtras state of mind. Dhritarashtras state of mind is Mamakaha Pandavah, his world is divided between mine and others.
Even his own brothers children, whom he has raised, he does not consider to be mine. So we know now that this division in our mind, this duality of I and mine versus the world outside of me, creates the conflict. All the conflicts, as we have discussed, are there because of this sense of duality and because of not following our own Dharma. Had Dhritarashtra followed his Dharma, we wouldnt have this war.
Bhagavan Ved Vyas is now painting the picture of how different people are situated in this Mahabharata. As we have heard many times before, all the characters and situations we encounter in life are already there in the Mahabharata. It is said that if it is not in Mahabharata, it is not worth even knowing or mentioning.
The situations we encounter in our life are already depicted somewhere in Mahabharata. So up till now, we have seen that Dhritarashtra said what he wanted to say, and we know that his world is divided into mine and Pandavas. Thats how he saw the world. Then we have seen Sanjaya narrating whats happening on the battlefield.
Sanjaya was the most loyal advisor to Dhritarashtra. He would obviously never go against Dhritarashtra or do anything to hurt him. As we know from Mahabharata, even when Dhritarashtra left for the forest after the war, Sanjaya went with him.
He was there until they were caught in the forest fire. I think Dhritarashtra asked him to leave, so he leaves and saves himself. But Dhritarashtra and Gandhari decided they were not going to leave.
He was there till the end of his life. But Sanjaya was not a yes-man. As somebody said, if you hire the next guy, dont hire a yes-man, you will be in trouble.
So Sanjaya was a loyal advisor but not a yes-man. Therefore he gave the narration of whats happening as he saw it. As we have seen, first he describes how Duryodhana acted in that situation.
He wasnt fully confident. He was evaluating the strength of each army, whether its good enough or not good enough. And then we have seen that Bhishma declared the war and the Pandavas responded.
But the leader of the Pandavas responding was not one of the General but Madhava himself. The Krishna himself responded first. Krishna had already decided there is no other way but to fight this war to settle the score.
So Krishna responded and all Pandavas followed enthusiastically. So you can see that the Pandavas are enthusiastic and confident about their own ability and in their cause. It also gives us an indication.
As long as you are sure about the cause of your pursuits you will be confident. And then we have seen the reaction from Gauravas side which Sanjay narrates. Its not that we are adding anything here but he never said anything about what happened in the Pandavas side.
He only said whats happened on the Dhritarashtra side. And he said this great sound which reverberated between the earth and the sky made the hearts of the people in Dhritarashtra army shiver. He didnt say that for the Pandavas.
This gives an indication that if youre not sure about your cause, any obstacle will make you unsettled. You will not be sure whether this is the right thing to do or not. On the Pandava side, Sanjaya has not given that indication.
He saw only the enthusiastic response to Bhishmas call for the war. So we can take a few lessons from here. As long as youre sure about your pursuits, no matter what obstacles arise, you will be confident and you will pursue your path towards your goal.
If youre not sure, even the smallest obstacle will make you rethink: Is this the right thing to do? Am I really putting my energy in the right place? Will I be able to win in this situation? Bhagavan Vedavyasa through Sanjayas narration is painting this picture of how things work. When we are facing this battle of life, after everyone has expressed their opinion by blowing their own conch, each one has to have their own opinion in life. No matter what other people have said. Shankhan dadhmuh prithak prithak, each one has to say I support it or I dont support it. So one who is not saying anything, we know that hes on the fence.
But each one gave their own opinion that they support this pursuit. On the Pandava side we are seeing enthusiastic support; on the Kaurava side, Sanjaya wants to give the correct report to Dhritarashtra because he is the king. And maybe Bhagavan Vedavyasa had a little bias because he had tried in the beginning to stop this war by convincing Dhritarashtra in a last-ditch effort.
But it obviously did not work. So verse 19 says: Sa ghosha Dhartarashtranaam hridayani vyadarayat, nabhas cha prithivim chaiva tumulo abhyanunadadayan, that tumultuous sound which reverberated between the sky and the earth rent the hearts of Dhritarashtras army. Verse 20: Atha vyavasthitan drishtva Dhartarashtran Kapidhvaja, pravritte shastra sampate dhanuhu udyamya Pandava. Sanjaya now focuses on Arjuna.
We have learned from Mahabharata that Sanjaya had this unique vision, not only could he see things, but he could also read peoples minds and see things beyond normal perception. In fact, before this war starts, Sanjayas vision was tested by Bhagavan Vedavyasa and Dhritarashtra. Sanjaya described distant lands which he had never visited before, the people, the culture, and all the fauna and flora of those lands.
So he had this great ability to see things which are not within normal perception. So now hes focusing on Arjuna, describing what Arjuna is doing and saying. Thus having seen the Kaurava army arranged in formation, Kapidhvaja, Arjunas chariot was called Kapidhvaja because his emblem on his flag was Hanuman.
Hanuman was very devoted to Bhagavan Ramachandra, and he said, In any age, at any time, wherever there is Rama, I will be there. Krishna being Ramas incarnation, Hanuman is always there when Krishna is involved in a battle. So Arjunas chariot is called Kapidhvaja. Thus, having seen the Kaurava army now arranged in formation, with all the weapons ready to be discharged, Dhanuhu udyamya, he picked up his bow, getting ready.
Here Sanjaya addresses Dhritarashtra as Mahipate, O Lord of the Earth. Having seen all this, Arjuna said this to Hrishikesha, Krishna. Arjuna uvacha, now Arjuna speaks. Anytime somebody speaks or opens their mouth, we know whats going on in their mind. Thats why we have this fear of public speaking.
Because as long as I keep my mouth shut, you dont know whats going on. Am I a Democrat or Republican or Independent? But as soon as I open my mouth, you know. These days you can also tell what channel someones watching, MSNBC or Fox News.
So up till now, Arjuna has not said anything. He just blew his conch. So we know he is very confident, very enthusiastic.
I wouldnt call him arrogant, I would call him very confident in his pursuit, in what he is going to do, and in his ability. He picks up his bow, ready, I am ready and capable. And then he said: Arjuna uvacha, senayoho ubhayoho madhye ratham sthapaya me Achyuta, O Achyuta, place this chariot in the midst of the two armies, right in the middle.
He addresses Krishna as Achyuta, one who never wavers from his position. That this is the iconic image we have of Krishna and Arjuna in the chariot. This reminds students of the Upanishads of the parable of the chariot in Katha Upanishad: this body is the chariot and the atma is the rider.
Buddhi is the charioteer, the mind is the reins, and the senses are the horses. The sense objects create the path on which the chariot moves. The senses are running on that path, the mind is the reins.
In the hands of Buddhi, along with the senses, the rider, the ego, becomes the enjoyer. The ego is the rider and the senses are drawing this chariot towards the sense objects. As long as that Buddhi is pure and in control, the chariot will be in control.
If the Buddhi is not purified, it will let the senses go in the wrong direction. So here Arjuna tells Krishna to put his chariot right in the middle of the two armies. Because Yavat etan nirikshey aham yoddhu kaman avasthitan, kairmaya saha yoddhavyam asmin rana samudyame, I want to see who are desirous to fight in this battle.
I want to make sure that I know whom I am fighting. Its basically due diligence. Anytime we have to go for an interview, the first thing someone might ask is, Rajan, did you find out who were competing against? I said I never asked that question because half the time they dont give that answer.
But we are very curious to see who we are competing against. Im sure Arjuna knew, but he wanted to make sure. Lets see on the very first day who is there.
Verse 23: Dhartarashtrasya durbuddhe yuddhe priya chikirsava, I want to see those who are assembled here to fight, wishing to please in battle the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra. We now see Arjunas state of mind, very confident, and he has great animosity toward Duryodhana, calling him evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra. He also knows that the people who are there are not fighting a righteous battle, they just want to please Duryodhana. Thats why they are there.
Because Duryodhana has the power, he is the person in charge of the entire empire. And they want to be in his good graces, in his good books. Therefore they are there.
So let me see who those people are whom Ill be fighting. Its basically as simple as that. Thats what we have seen so far.

Verse 19 reveals a crucial psychological truth: the tumultuous sound from the Pandava side rent the hearts (hridayani vyadarayat) of Dhritarashtras army. When youre uncertain about your cause, even the opponents confidence becomes threatening. The Kauravas had more soldiers, more resources, yet their hearts were shaken by sound alone. This shows how inner doubt magnifies external challenges. Notice also the contrasting states of the two sides. Sanjaya reports no heart-rending fear on the Pandava side, only enthusiastic response to the call. When youre sure about your purpose, obstacles dont destabilize you. When youre not sure, even small setbacks cause doubt. Reflect honestly: in your current challenges, are you more like the confident Pandavas or the anxious Kauravas? Then comes Arjuna in verse 20-21, described as Kapidhvaja, one whose flag bears Hanuman. This isnt just decoration; Hanuman promised to be present wherever Rama (and his incarnation Krishna) fights for dharma. Arjuna, supremely confident, picks up his bow and commands: Achyuta, place my chariot between the two armies. He addresses Krishna as Achyuta, the one who never wavers. But heres the irony: Arjuna himself is about to waver profoundly. The one who calls on the Unwavering One is about to demonstrate just how much humans can shake. This week, notice when you invoke stability and certainty in others precisely because you sense your own approaching instability. Sometimes our strongest declarations of confidence come just before our deepest crises of doubt.
